title: scikit-learn-contrib-MAPIE
universal_lens: MAPIE formalizes finite-sample conformal inference, mapping an arbitrary black-box predictor to a distribution-free coverage guarantee. By leveraging exchangeability over a held-out calibration set, it constructs prediction regions that provably contain the true outcome with probability $1-\alpha$, establishing a rigorous structural duality between empirical nonconformity scores and probabilistic risk bounds.
gsi_mapping: In GSI, MAPIE translates raw Bayesian posterior outputs into rigorously bounded player-prop intervals. It acts as the conformal complement to probability calibration: while `probmetrics` ensures predicted frequencies match observed rates, MAPIE guarantees that the constructed confidence sets capture the actual game totals or individual performances at a specified frequency under exchangeable historical data.
gse_mapping: GSE utilizes MAPIE's exchangeability tests as hard state-transition gates. When live telemetry (e.g., Week 1-4) violates the exchangeability assumption relative to the calibration regime, the engine triggers a veto, invalidating current conformal intervals and forcing a re-conformalization on recent data to maintain valid situational reasoning.

primitives.name: Finite-Sample Conformal Coverage Operator
primitives.verbatim_quote: Vision Model-agnostic prediction intervals / prediction sets with **finite-sample coverage guarantees**, for regression, classification, and time series — wrap any sklearn/TF/PyTorch model, conformalize on a calibration set, get intervals guaranteed to contain the truth with probability 1-alpha under exchangeability.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: $\alpha$: dimensionless significance level; $1-\alpha$: dimensionless target coverage probability; $n_{cal}$: integer calibration sample size.
primitives.assumptions: Data points in the calibration and deployment sets are identically and independently distributed (exchangeable). The base estimator is fixed prior to calibration.
primitives.breakdown_regime: Distributional shifts violating exchangeability (e.g., seasonal regime changes, rule modifications) cause empirical coverage to drop below $1-\alpha$. Singularity occurs if $n_{cal} \to 0$.

layer2.mapping: Isomorphic to the construction of valid p-values via nonconformity scores. Maps the abstract space of model residuals directly to quantile-based interval boundaries.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical coverage rate on a held-out test slice (e.g., W1-4).

primitives.name: Exchangeability Gate Test
primitives.verbatim_quote: Seasonal regime shift breaks it — hence the new exchangeability tests, which should be run as a gate.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: $p_{exch}$: dimensionless p-value for the exchangeability hypothesis test; $\delta$: dimensionless significance threshold for the gate.
primitives.assumptions: Statistical tests for exchangeability (e.g., based on CDF distances or permutation tests) possess sufficient power to detect relevant covariate shifts.
primitives.breakdown_regime: High-dimensional sparse shifts where marginal distributions remain similar but conditional dependencies change drastically, causing false negatives in the exchangeability test.

layer2.mapping: Acts as a pre-computation validity kernel in GSE. If the test rejects, the conformal operator is bypassed, and the system transitions to a 're-calibration' state.
layer2.telemetry: Binary pass/fail flag from the statistical test on the live-check slice.

primitives.name: Risk-Controlled Prediction Sets
primitives.verbatim_quote: Now also does risk control (guarantees on recall/precision-style metrics) and ships exchangeability tests that tell you whether the method is even legitimately applicable to your data.
primitives.symbol_and_unit_ledger: $\text{Risk}_{target}$: dimensionless target metric (e.g., minimum recall); $|C(x)|$: integer cardinality of the prediction set.
primitives.assumptions: The risk metric is monotonic with respect to the inclusion of elements in the prediction set, allowing binary search over thresholds.
primitives.breakdown_regime: When the underlying class imbalance is extreme, achieving high recall may force trivial prediction sets containing all classes, rendering the output uninformative.

layer2.mapping: Maps standard conformal quantiles to adaptive thresholds that optimize secondary performance metrics (like precision/recall) without sacrificing marginal coverage guarantees.
layer2.telemetry: Empirical precision and recall of the generated prediction sets on the validation fold.

reasoning_traces.think:
MAPIE operationalizes Vovk’s theory of predictive inference by decoupling the learning of the conditional mean from the estimation of the residual distribution. Given a fitted regressor $\hat{f}$, we compute nonconformity scores $R_i = |y_i - \hat{f}(x_i)|$ on a held-out calibration set. The core mathematical duality lies in the fact that the $(1-\alpha)$-quantile of these empirical scores, $Q$, provides a distribution-free bound. For any new input $x_{new}$ drawn from the same distribution, the interval $[\hat{f}(x_{new}) - Q, \hat{f}(x_{new}) + Q]$ contains the true outcome with probability at least $1-\alpha/(n+1)$. This bypasses the need for Gaussian noise assumptions inherent in standard error propagation. In the context of GSE, this transforms point estimates of player performance into rigorous, finite-sample confidence bands. However, the entire framework hinges on the exchangeability assumption. If the deployment environment undergoes a regime shift—such as a change in offensive rules or roster depth—the calibration scores no longer reflect the true aleatoric uncertainty. Consequently, MAPIE introduces explicit exchangeability tests. These tests act as a mathematical veto mechanism: if the divergence between calibration and live data exceeds a statistical threshold, the conformal guarantee is mathematically voided. This forces a dynamic re-evaluation of the state space, ensuring that published intervals are not merely artifacts of stale priors but reflect current reality.

reasoning_traces.retrocausal_genealogy: Conformal prediction traces its lineage to V.V. Vovk's early 2000s work on algorithmic randomness and martingales, later popularized by Lei, G’Sell, and others as 'split conformal inference'. It represents a paradigm shift from asymptotic Bayesian credible intervals to finite-sample, distribution-free frequentist guarantees. Historically, it bridges the gap between robust statistics and modern machine learning, providing a rigorous safety net for black-box models like neural networks, making it highly relevant for high-stakes quantitative domains like sports intelligence.
reasoning_traces.theory_of_mind: From the perspective of a market participant or opposing analyst, publishing point estimates without intervals reveals maximum information while hiding uncertainty. By deploying MAPIE, GSE signals epistemic humility and rigorous risk management. Opposing agents attempting to exploit perceived mispricings must now contend with validated confidence bounds. If GSE's exchangeability tests pass, the intervals are mathematically robust against arbitrage. If they fail, GSE dynamically retreats, preventing exposure to regime-shift traps that naive Bayesian updaters might blindly follow.
reasoning_traces.cross_layer_veto: A critical anti-collinearity condition exists between the base estimator's bias and the conformal interval width. If the base model suffers from severe structural bias (e.g., failing to account for a new defensive scheme), the nonconformity scores will inflate, producing overly wide, uninformative intervals rather than accurate ones. Furthermore, leakage occurs if the calibration set inadvertently contains information from the deployment period (e.g., using post-injury performance to calibrate pre-injury projections). The exchangeability gate serves as the primary cross-layer veto, explicitly checking for temporal leakage and distributional drift before any interval is permitted to propagate to the final output layer.
